items.title: [elpais.com] Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems fuel concerns about connected household appliances
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Cyberattacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems in supermarkets and French blood banks have destroyed food in Europe and heightened concerns about connected devices. Nearly 800 freezers were sabotaged in France and Northern Europe this week. On November 2, temperatures also rose in the cold rooms of a blood donation service in France. There, alarms and swift action prevented damage to stored blood. The targeted systems used internet-accessible controls for maintenance and remote operation. According to experts, similar attacks on private smart-home devices are less likely because, with typical router configurations, the devices cannot be accessed directly from the internet. Risks include outdated software, weak passwords, and devices with cameras or microphones. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security recommends automatic updates, separate networks for smart-home devices, and unique passwords. The identity of those behind the attacks remains unclear.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Grok Build exposes 35,578 apps, leaking sensitive company data
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Security researchers found that 35,578 of 37,571 web apps built with SpaceXSI’s Grok Build, a chat-based app builder, were accessible without signing in, exposing business and personal information at SpaceXSI and 30 other organizations. Claroc, the security firm that found the apps, estimated that about one in 10 accessible apps contained internal or personal data and roughly 2% held material it rated high or critical in severity. Exposed material included a SpaceXSI sales map covering 594 strategic accounts, a hospital directory listing more than 3,500 employees, an intensive-care briefing about a patient and a timesheet with 18 users’ passwords in its code. The apps’ addresses were discoverable through searchable passive DNS records, and Grok Build preselected “Anyone with the link” as the sharing option in the researchers’ test. SpaceXSI removed 24 apps made by its own staff and X employees; Claroc said other users’ apps remained available and that it had begun contacting affected organizations.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Singapore urges firms to secure refrigeration controls after European hacks
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency (CSA) urged organizations on Nov. 6 to restrict internet access to operational technology controls, including refrigeration systems, after cyberattacks on supermarket cooling systems and French blood-storage equipment. CSA said it had received no reports of comparable incidents in Singapore. The Singapore Food Agency said the attacks had not disrupted the country’s food supply and it was checking with retailers and cold-chain warehouses. The advisory follows a Nov. 5 warning from five U.S. agencies that attackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controllers worldwide. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said it found more than 5,000 internet-exposed devices from manufacturers named in a French cybersecurity advisory on Nov. 5-6; the firm cautioned that exposure alone does not show a device was vulnerable. Censys separately counted 6,695 exposed controllers on Oct. 9 and 3,124 still accessible on Nov. 5. European Union agencies said affected member states were investigating and sharing information after another wave of attacks on Nov. 1-2. The perpetrators remain unidentified. Pro-Russian groups have claimed responsibility, but those claims are unverified, and the Kremlin denied Russian involvement.

India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned financial firms that an active campaign it calls Crafty Falcon is targeting non-bank lenders, fintech companies, payment providers and cryptocurrency exchanges. The agency has not publicly identified who is behind the attacks or attributed them to a state. Attackers use publicly available AI-assisted tools to find exposed applications, application programming interfaces (APIs) and privileged access, then misuse victims’ own payment systems to transfer funds. CERT-In says attacks have continued against organizations that did not fully address earlier weaknesses, with intrusions timed for weekends and holidays when monitoring may be reduced. According to a police complaint, two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders lost about $2 million in more than 700 unauthorized transfers on Oct. 8 and 9 after attackers compromised APIs. Reports on that incident did not establish a link to Crafty Falcon.

items.content_html:

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began (sciencefeatured.com). The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity (sciencefeatured.com). The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions (sciencefeatured.com). Study sample: The analysis included several thousand participants with healthy memory and thinking abilities at the outset; models accounted for factors including education, smoking, depression and chronic illness (sciencefeatured.com). Cognitive tests: Participants completed word-list recall tests to assess memory and counting and subtraction tasks to assess executive function (sciencefeatured.com). Exercise research: Montreal neuropsychologist Louis Bherer said participants in his lab’s physical and cognitive exercise programs showed improvements in attention and response speed after training, while memory changes took longer (nautil.us).

items.title: [news.mit.edu] Older adults show weaker brain-clearing fluid waves during sleep
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

MIT researchers found that older adults had significantly weaker waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which helps clear waste from the brain during sleep, than younger adults. The researchers used brain imaging and electroencephalography to study volunteers ages 18 to 39 and 60 to 84, linking the reduced flow partly to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and diminished vascular responses. Separately, a study described in a paper shared on Reddit found that LSD-related gene-expression patterns in rats and mice ran counter to some patterns associated with human brain aging. LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people.

LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people (reddit.com). Vascular tests: In awake participants, older adults showed smaller blood-flow responses to both a flickering checkerboard and breath-holding, which raises carbon dioxide levels (mit.edu, nautil.us). Unexplained gap: The measured vascular changes accounted for much, but not all, of the age-related difference in CSF flow, leaving some of the difference unexplained (mit.edu, nautil.us). Preclinical LSD: The LSD study compared data from chronic dosing in rats and acute multi-dose testing in mice with human aging-related gene-expression datasets. It also tested amyloid-beta effects in primary mouse cortical cultures (reddit.com).

items.title: [Small Farm Canada] Could Earlier Shearing Help Produce Bigger, Healthier Lambs?
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Could changing when you shear pregnant ewes lead to heavier lambs? New research points to promising results among ewes carrying twins and triplets, although cold-climate producers should take some important precautions.
